title: Narrative Transportation: Why Stories Persuade Better Than Fact Lists
explainer: Psychologists Melanie Green and Timothy Brock's research on 'narrative transportation' found that when readers become absorbed in a story - picturing its scenes, following a protagonist through a problem - they come away remembering it longer, adopting its conclusions more readily, and scrutinizing its claims less critically than when given the same information as a plain list of facts. Notably, their experiments found this effect held even when readers were told upfront that a story was fictional, suggesting it's the immersion itself doing the persuasive work, not the story's factual authority. That is the cognitive mechanism behind why a project write-up that puts a reader inside a concrete problem, a decision point, and a moment of change lands harder than an equivalent bullet list of features and technologies used.

resources.title: The role of transportation in the persuasiveness of public narratives (Green & Brock, 2000)
